extracted.intended_audience: research funders, research policy-makers, grant administrators, and researchers studying peer review and funding allocation
extracted.subtask_description: Realist-synthesis evidence and recommendations about interventions to improve peer review and decision-making for research grant funding, including classification of interventions, examples of effective practices, and cautions about unintended consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific, economic and social benefit of research
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate proposals for their scientific contribution as well as the economic and social benefits they will deliver to stakeholders outside academia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as one of the common themes interventions should address; funders are encouraged to consider wider societal relevance when setting priorities and assessing proposals. No specific scoring rubric provided, but interventions that increase relevance (e.g., audition systems linking ideas to funders) are discussed as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Researcher career stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the extent to which funding and decision-making practices support stable careers for researchers, particularly early-career researchers (ECRs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interventions that reduce burden (shorter applications, training) and promote ECRs were noted as positive consequences; funders should weigh career-impact when designing schemes and quotas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding of innovative research
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritise and design mechanisms specifically to identify and fund high-innovation/high-risk research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include NIH High-Risk, High-Reward programs, Pioneer Awards, sandpits, randomisation, and 'Golden tickets'. The paper suggests combining incremental process improvements with innovative decision methods to increase innovation in funded research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and accountability of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure reviewer selection processes produce competent, accountable reviewers and mitigate conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites work on selecting competent referees and the use of reviewer registers; recommendations include reviewer training and mechanisms for accountability. Beware reviewer fatigue and overuse of frequent reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of reviewers to proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign appropriate reviewers to proposals using structured processes or tools to match expertise and reduce mismatch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References semi-automatic web tools and reviewer-register-based selection; allocation influences reliability and fairness of review outcome and is a distinct intervention target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and reliability of review
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the methodological quality and inter-rater reliability of peer review for funding decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence supports reviewer training to improve inter-rater reliability and internal peer review systems to improve submissions. Publishing review scores was listed as an intervention that demonstrated long-term positive outcomes. The paper stresses need for robust evidence (RCTs, prospective/feasibility studies) to assess effects on quality/reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient and Public Involvement (PPI) in research funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Include patients, advocates and other non-academic stakeholders in the assessment and decision-making process for funding, often via a two-tier system (experts + other stakeholders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple interventions promoting PPI restructured peer review into experts and other stakeholders; examples (PCORI, CURES) showed increased relevance of funded research. Guidance notes many PPI interventions require structural change and careful evaluation of mechanisms and contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unnecessary burden on applicants, reviewers and funders
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimise administrative and time burden across the funding cycle for applicants, reviewers and funders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The literature places heavy emphasis on burden reduction. Effective interventions included shortening applications, training applicants, streamlining review timelines, and simplifying decision categories. Trade-offs and unintended downstream burdens (e.g., due to submission quotas) must be assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training applicants in grant writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide training to applicants to improve proposal quality and increase positive long-term outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified as an intervention demonstrating long-term positive outcomes: training equipped applicants with better knowledge of peer review, reduced writing burden, and improved submissions. No precise curriculum given; training is recommended as part of capacity-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing review scores (transparency of review outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish reviewer scores to increase transparency and potentially improve review quality and accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as an intervention with positive outcomes. The paper implies publishing scores can help accountability and learning, but does not specify format or limits; implementers should monitor for unintended effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involving patients and health advocates in decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively include patient/advocate perspectives in grant selection to increase relevance and innovation of funded research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence from multiple studies (e.g., consumer inclusion in breast cancer proposal review) shows quantitative and qualitative impacts. Often involves restructuring panels and decision processes; requires training and clear roles for non-expert stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission quotas
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit the number of applications an institution or individual may submit to reduce demand on review systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implemented by NSF and others to limit funding demand. While it can reduce reviewer burden and application volumes, the paper highlights unintended consequences (e.g., extra internal HEI competitions, increased applicant administrative work) and recommends working with HEIs to mitigate downstream effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shortening applications and focused application content
rubrics_metrics.description: Use shorter application forms focused on essential items (e.g., research question, methods, budget, expected impact, partnerships) to speed review and reduce burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: AusHSI two-month process used 1200-word applications and a simplified review system ('reject', 'revise', 'accept to interview'), resulting in rapid shortlisting and reduced emphasis on track record. Short forms can reduce time-to-decision and may benefit ECRs, but funders should pilot and evaluate effects on decision quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporating sandpits, randomisation, and 'Golden tickets'
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt alternative decision mechanisms (e.g., creative workshops, lotteries, special discretionary awards) to surface novel ideas and reduce biases of standard peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These mechanisms were used in selected calls and are cited as contributing to increased innovation and reduced inter-rater variability in some contexts. They are recommended as optional, experimental tools rather than wholesale replacements of peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtual panels and teleconference review
rubrics_metrics.description: Use remote/virtual panels instead of face-to-face meetings to reduce costs and logistical burdens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtual panels were among interventions with positive outcomes (reduced cost, time); the paper references comparative studies (teleconference vs face-to-face) showing effects on review outcomes and recommends evaluation of trade-offs in deliberation quality versus efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modifying composition of review and decision panels
rubrics_metrics.description: Change panel membership (e.g., include diverse expertise, rotate members, include ad hoc reviewers) to improve decision-making and reduce undue influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing panel composition was a commonly implemented incremental change. The paper notes ad hoc reviewers can diversify opinions but may cause excessive reviewer service if mismanaged; policies on reviewer benefits and rotation should be monitored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of software and decision tools for applicant shortlisting
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ automated or semi-automated decision tools (e.g., algorithms based on productivity metrics) to support shortlisting of applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Spanish SRA's Ramón y Cajal scheme modelling showed software could identify 'good' applicants based on productivity alone, prompting recommendation to optimise decision tools to support shortlisting. Caution: such tools may reflect known biases (age, gender); funders should optimise and audit tools to avoid embedding bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of interventions by level of change
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame interventions as impact-oriented (benefit outside academia), organisation-level (internal processes/structures), or incremental (changes to specific parts of peer review and decision-making).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper organises interventions into these categories to guide funders in selecting appropriate interventions given their goals and capacity. Use this framework to plan pilots and scale-up with attention to scope and stakeholders affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine incremental changes with innovative interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a mixed approach of improving specific mechanisms within peer review while piloting novel decision methods to achieve longer-term impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors argue that incremental improvements (e.g., shortening applications, changing panel composition) plus selective innovation (e.g., sandpits, lotteries) may be the most realistic route to sustainable, generalisable improvements. Evaluate combinations rather than single changes in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous evaluation and transparency (publish pilots, build open databases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuously evaluate implemented interventions, publish outcomes of pilots, and create open resources to encourage shared learning and accountability among funders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations include building an open database of funder peer review processes, publishing pilot outcomes, and forming consortia of funders. This supports evidence accumulation and cross-organisational learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use robust study designs to evaluate interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate strong evidence (RCTs, prospective or feasibility studies) to determine the efficacy and generalisability of interventions to peer review and funding decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The synthesis found much of the literature was theoretical; the authors recommend more robust empirical research to support causal claims and inform scale-up decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and manage unintended consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly consider and monitor for downstream or cross-stakeholder unintended consequences when designing and implementing interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: submission quotas created internal HEI burdens; ad hoc reviewer policies increased excessive service. The paper stresses working with affected stakeholders (HEIs, reviewers) to anticipate trade-offs and adapt policies accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplified decision categories in initial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Use coarse initial reviewer decisions (e.g., 'reject', 'revise', 'accept to interview') to streamline shortlisting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in the AusHSI accelerated process alongside short applications; facilitated rapid decisions and reduced administrative burden. Advice: pair with clear criteria for each category and rapid timelines for feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce emphasis on applicant track record in some processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Design some funding routes to place less weight on applicant CVs and track records, thereby potentially benefiting ECRs and diversifying funded applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed as an unintended (but positive) consequence of short application formats and streamlined review. Funders should consider when reduced emphasis is appropriate and monitor effects on selection quality and equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer training to improve review quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide structured training to reviewers to improve the consistency, fairness, and reliability of peer review judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited evidence (e.g., randomized trials) that training can improve review quality and inter-rater reliability. Training is recommended both for external reviewers and internal peer-review processes used by funders.
